rv.q: Because what its creators have whipped up is an unlikely but scrumptious blend of cheese and caviar.
Honeymoon in Vegas is too damn fun to keep secret.
"Honeymoon in Vegas," based on the 1992 film, is an unexpectedly delightful, thoroughly conventional movie spinoff that isn't hard-selling anything more than a good time created by experts.

This cheerfully mindless musical comedy about a mama's boy who loses his fiancee in a poker game is so relentlessly upbeat that it's hard to resist its charms, even when your brain is screaming at you to show some taste.
Things start dragging when Tommy enters the picture.
You’ll even forgive yourself for enjoying the ride.
It’s breezy and fun, full of toe-tapping numbers, witty design touches and frequent bursts of irreverent comic inspiration.
At times Honeymoon in Vegas, particularly in its swinging Rat Pack score by Jason Robert Brown, is a jolting reminder of the very entertaining, somewhat risqué musicals of the 1950s and 1960s.
Will audiences see past what this show asks them to overlook?
The first act is gloriously fine, the second act much less so—but some of the show’s biggest problems stem from some of the casting rather than from the adaptation.
Drab sets, bad politics and wince-inducing stereotypes sink this threadbare production, in which Tony Danza steals scenes but can’t save them.
Honeymoon In Vegas hits the musical comedy jackpot.

"It’s a great surprise that the large-scale musical version of the movie is a frothy delight, a pineapple-sweet warm-up in this most frigid season...Vegas has its share of missteps—a few clunker lines, a still-slightly-sexist undertone, and what has to be the only showtune in history about skin cancer.
Brown’s legion of fans are apt to consider this one of his finer achievements, in spite of the source material’s garish qualities.
Thankfully, given a strong score by Jason Robert Brown, fleet of foot direction by Gary Griffin, and knockout performances by its two leads, Honeymoon is much, much better than it has a right to be.
Yet, taken as a whole, the evening lacks momentum — that inspired energy that pulls you into what's happening on a stage.
Sad to say, the show also needs some radical recasting.

But more often than not, “Honeymoon in Vegas” is mired in a pained attempt to enliven and exaggerate a simple but heartfelt boy-meets-girl/boy-loses-girl story into a broad, over-the-top musical comedy.
It’s too bad Danza throws this Honeymoon off balance.
As is, the show, directed by Gary Griffin (“The Color Purple”) is cute and old-fashioned, a good time.
As empty-calorie musicals go, you could do worse than this Honeymoon.

cn.t: This old-fashioned musical comedy divides critics, who praise Jason Robert Brown's brassy score and Tony Danza's performance but fault its dated humor and uneven execution. Most find it pleasant, conventional fun that doesn't quite soar.

vs.sum: An older theater in need of renovation, with virtually no rake in the orchestra — a tall person seated in front will block your view. First mezzanine row has a horizontal safety bar that partially obstructs sightlines. Legroom is tight throughout.

acc.note: Step-free main entrance to Orchestra. 6 wheelchair spaces. Personal induction loop devices available.
